items.prompt: Given the root of a binary tree, decide whether every node's key is larger than all keys in its left subtree and smaller than all keys in its right subtree.
items.why: It's the BST invariant over whole subtrees → carry (lo, hi) bounds down, or check that the in-order walk is strictly increasing.

items.prompt: Return the average value of the nodes on each level of a binary tree.
items.why: "Each level" → level-order traversal with a queue, processing one level's size at a time.

items.prompt: Given the root of a BST, return its k-th smallest key.
items.why: The tree is already a BST, so an in-order walk yields sorted keys. Stop at the k-th one, O(h + k). A heap would ignore the ordering you already have.

items.prompt: Return the largest sum of any path between two nodes of a binary tree (the path need not pass through the root; values may be negative).
items.why: The answer can sit anywhere and combines both children → post-order that returns a one-sided gain and records the two-sided candidate.

items.prompt: Given a list of words, answer many queries of the form "how many words start with this prefix?".
items.why: Shared-prefix queries over many strings → a trie, where each node is a prefix and stores how many words pass through it.

items.prompt: Return every root-to-leaf path whose values add up to a target.
items.why: Enumerating root-to-leaf paths with a growing/shrinking path list is the DFS-with-backtracking template.

items.prompt: Given a BST and two keys in it, find the deepest node that has both keys in its subtree.
items.why: LCA in a BST → walk down from the root: both smaller go left, both larger go right, otherwise this node splits them. O(h).

items.prompt: Numbers arrive one by one; after each, report the k-th largest seen so far.
items.why: Streaming k-th largest → a size-k min-heap. A hand-rolled balanced BST would work but isn't the expected tool.

items.prompt: Decide whether a binary tree is height-balanced (subtree heights differ by at most one at every node) in a single pass.
items.why: "At every node, compare the children" → a post-order that returns a summary (the height) to the parent, instead of recomputing heights from every node.

items.prompt: Edges between computers are added one at a time; after each addition, report how many separate networks there are.
items.why: Incremental connectivity → union-find over parent pointers. Re-running a traversal after every edge is too slow.
